profile.headline: Alphavirus of the Semliki Forest complex causing explosive epidemics of febrile polyarthritis.
profile.syndrome: Sudden high fever with severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia and rash; the name means 'that which bends up'. Arthritis persists for months to years in 30–40%. Neonatal infection from intrapartum transmission and neurological disease in older adults can be severe; deaths occur mainly via decompensation of comorbidity.
profile.transmission: Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus. The A226V envelope mutation improved Ae. albopictus transmission and drove epidemic spread outside the tropics.
profile.reservoir: Humans in epidemics; non-human primates in African sylvatic cycles.
profile.geography: Africa, Asia, Indian Ocean, Americas since 2013, with autochthonous outbreaks in southern Europe.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR in the first week (viraemia is high), IgM thereafter.
profile.management: Analgesia and physiotherapy; chronic arthritis may need rheumatological care.
profile.prevention: Vector control; the virus-like particle vaccine Vimkunya is licensed from 12 years of age. The live-attenuated IXCHIQ was licensed first, but its US licence was suspended in August 2025 and the application withdrawn in January 2026 after vaccine-strain encephalitis and other serious adverse events.
evidence: High-titre viraemia readily detected in patients; laboratory-confirmed epidemics affecting millions.

geo.text: Africa, Asia, Indian Ocean, Americas since 2013, with autochthonous outbreaks in southern Europe.

profile.headline: The most commonly notified arboviral infection in Australia.
profile.syndrome: Epidemic polyarthritis: symmetrical joint pain and swelling, rash and fatigue, often lasting months. No deaths attributed.
profile.geography: Australia, Papua New Guinea, Pacific islands.
profile.diagnosis: IgM/IgG serology; RT-PCR rarely positive by presentation.
evidence: Thousands of serologically confirmed notifications annually with a well-defined clinical syndrome.

names: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV), subtypes IAB/IC/ID/IE
profile.headline: Epizootic alphavirus causing large human and equine outbreaks in the Americas; also a classical laboratory-acquired infection.
profile.syndrome: Influenza-like illness with fever, headache, myalgia and prostration in most; encephalitis in ~4% of children and <1% of adults. Infection in pregnancy can cause fetal loss.
profile.transmission: Mosquito-borne (many genera); highly infectious by aerosol, which accounts for laboratory-acquired cases.
profile.reservoir: Equines amplify epizootic subtypes; rodents maintain enzootic subtypes.
profile.geography: Central and South America, with historical incursions into Texas.
profile.prevention: Equine vaccination (which interrupts amplification), vector control, and biosafety containment in laboratories.
evidence: Human isolations from thousands of cases during the 1962–1971 and 1995 epidemics; documented aerosol laboratory infections.

refs.label: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus: the problem is not over for tropical America. Ann Clin Microbiol Antimicrob 2020
Current Understanding of the Molecular Basis of Venezuelan Equine Encephalitis Virus Pathogenesis and Vaccine Development. Viruses 2019

profile.headline: The most lethal arbovirus endemic to North America.
profile.syndrome: Encephalitis with fulminant onset; case fatality ~30% and severe neurological sequelae in most survivors. Infection is rare but outbreaks cluster around freshwater swamp habitats.
profile.transmission: Culiseta melanura maintains the bird cycle; bridge vectors (Coquillettidia, Aedes, Culex) infect humans and horses.
profile.reservoir: Passerine birds in freshwater hardwood swamps.
profile.geography: Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States, Great Lakes region, Caribbean.
profile.diagnosis: CSF/serum IgM; RT-PCR on brain tissue; MRI shows basal ganglia and thalamic lesions.
profile.management: Supportive intensive care; no specific therapy.
profile.prevention: Mosquito avoidance and aerial larviciding during amplification; equine vaccine available, none for humans.
evidence: Virologically and histopathologically confirmed fatal human encephalitis over many decades.
